📖 UNDERSTANDING THE YIELD CURVE

The yield curve shows interest rates across different bond maturities. Think of it as a temperature check for the economy.

Normal curve: Long-term bonds pay more than short-term ones. Investors want extra reward for locking money up longer. This signals healthy economic expectations.

Inverted curve: Short-term rates exceed long-term rates. This happens when markets expect economic trouble ahead. The last three inversions preceded recessions in 2001, 2008, and 2020.

Flat curve: Little difference between short and long rates. Markets are uncertain about future direction.

Real example: Right now in August 2026, the US 2-year yields 4.1% while the 10-year sits at 4.3%. This mild steepening suggests markets expect moderate growth without overheating.

Why traders care:
- Banks profit less when curves flatten (borrow short, lend long)
- Inversions often trigger stock selloffs 6-18 months before recessions
- Currency traders watch curves for rate differential plays

PRO TIP: When the curve inverts, don't panic immediately. The recession signal typically plays out over 12-24 months. Use the warning to adjust position sizing and increase cash reserves gradually.


🏦 CENTRAL BANK BALANCE SHEETS DECODED

Central bank balance sheets reveal how much money authorities pump into or drain from the system. This matters more than most speeches.

The mechanics: When central banks buy bonds (QE), they create new money and expand their balance sheet. When they sell or let bonds mature (QT), money leaves the system and the balance sheet shrinks.

The Fed's balance sheet peaked at 9 trillion in 2022. By August 2026, it's down to 6.8 trillion through quantitative tightening. That's 2.2 trillion drained from markets.

The ECB currently holds 4.5 trillion euros in assets, still elevated from pandemic support programs.

Market impact examples:
- During 2020-2021 QE expansion, stocks rallied 70% as liquidity flooded in
- Since QT began in 2022, volatility increased and easy gains disappeared
- Bitcoin and tech stocks are most sensitive to balance sheet changes

Watch these signals:
- Balance sheet expansion = risk-on fuel
- Balance sheet contraction = tighter conditions
- Pace of change matters more than absolute size

SMART MONEY RULE: Track the rate of change in central bank balance sheets monthly. Aggressive expansion supports risk assets. Rapid contraction means reduce leverage and focus on quality.


💡 THREE FRIDAY TRADING TIPS

TIP 1 - PROTECT WEEKEND GAPS
Markets close for 48 hours. Geopolitical events don't. Cut position sizes by 30-50% before weekends if you're holding swing trades. The premium you lose on smaller positions is insurance against gap risk.

TIP 2 - END-OF-WEEK PROFIT TAKING
Fridays often see professionals lock in weekly gains between 2-4 PM EST. Don't chase momentum into the close. Better entry points usually appear Monday morning.

TIP 3 - REVIEW BEFORE YOU REST
Spend 15 minutes Friday evening reviewing your week. What worked? What didn't? Write down one lesson learned. Traders who journal consistently outperform those who don't by 12-18% annually according to trading psychology studies.


⚠️ MANAGING PORTFOLIO EXPOSURE

Portfolio exposure measures your total capital at risk across all positions. Many traders blow accounts by overexposing without realizing it.

The danger zones:
- Correlated positions that move together (holding five tech stocks isn't diversification)
- Hidden leverage through options or futures
- Concentration in single sectors during rotation events

Real scenario: A trader holds 40% portfolio in tech stocks, 20% in crypto, 15% in growth ETFs. Actual tech exposure? Over 75% when you account for overlap. One sector rotation wipes out months of gains.

Smart exposure rules:
- No single position over 5% of portfolio for beginners
- No single sector over 25% total exposure
- Keep 20-30% in cash or stable assets for opportunities
- Calculate true exposure including derivatives and correlations

August 2026 context: With technology stocks at high valuations and AI enthusiasm still running hot, many portfolios are dangerously overweight growth. Energy and healthcare offer uncorrelated alternatives.

The 50-30-20 framework:
- 50% core positions (diversified, lower risk)
- 30% conviction trades (higher risk, sized appropriately)
- 20% cash and defensive assets (opportunity fund)

RISK REMINDER: Exposure creep kills accounts slowly. Review your actual portfolio correlation monthly, not just individual positions. When everything moves together, you don't have diversification — you have concentrated risk wearing different costumes.
